speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to put it mildly, the first amendment is a technical one. It relates to that part of Bill C-84 which is not before us at the moment but is connected with Bill C-55. Bill C-84 has a provision empowering the Minister to turn away ships at sea under certain circumstances.
In the amendments being brought to Bill C-84 there is an amendment that would restrict the Minister from delegating that power. In other words, there is Clause 123 in the present Act which states, in effect, that the Minister may not delegate to any lower official powers under certain sections of the Act, and it lists those powers. The amendments to Bill C-84 would restrict the effect of that power, that is, restrict the Minister from delegating the power to turn away ships.
My Party and I are in agreement with that restriction. We are not in agreement with giving the Minister the power to turn away the ships, but we do at least agree that it should be restricted, if it is there, to the Minister only, for the reasons that the Senate and the Minister have agreed upon.
However, it has been pointed out to me from legal advice, and I say that only because it is obvious that I am not a legal expert or a lawyer, that the power to turn the ships away will come into effect when Bill C-84 is passed. But if that comes into effect after Bill C-55, then that restriction of the delegation would be cancelled because there is a section in Bill C-55 which provides for another restriction of the power of delegation, but not for that one. In other words, the restriction would not be in effect, even though that restriction was intended by the Senate when it considered that Bill and agreed to by the Minister in responding to the Bill.
The amendment that I am proposing, which I hope will be found acceptable by all sides, states:
"123.1. Should Bill C-84, entitled an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and the Criminal Code in consequence thereof, be assented to during the second session of the thirty-third Parliament and section 16 of that Act comes into force before this Act,-
In other words, if Bill C-54 were to be passed soon and Bill C-84 subsequently.
-then, on the day on which this Act comes into force the reference in section 123 of the Immigration Act, 1976 as amended by this Act, to paragraphs 19(1)(E) and (2)(A), subsections 39(2) and 40(1), subparagraph 48.01(1 )(E)(iii) and subsections 82.1(2) and 83(1) shall be read as a reference to paragraphs 19(1 )(E) and (2)(A), subsections 39(2) and 40(1), subparagraph 48.01 (1 )(E)(iii) and subsections 82.1(2), 83(1) and 91.1(1)."
I apologize, Madam Speaker, for the number of numbers and brackets, but this appears to be the legal situation that we have. I have sought the advice of the parliamentary staff on this matter, and received it, and I am grateful for that. I have sought advice of the Journals staff on this matter, as a matter of form, and received it, and I am grateful for that.
To simplify it for Hon. Members who may not have had the opportunity to follow this through in detail before now, it is the intention of the Senate and the Minister, agreed to, certainly by my Party and I believe by the other opposition Party, to restrict the power of the Minister to delegate authority to turn away ships. Even though that authority will lapse six months after Bill C-55 comes into force according to the amendments that are being considered, this particular aspect of it, this restriction of the delegating authority, would fail to operate from the time that Bill C-55 is declared until that lapse. Therefore, during that time the power of delegation of the Minister would exist. The Minister could delegate to lower officials the decision to turn away ships. Since that is not the intention of the Senate, nor the intention of the Minister, as I understand her amendments, I would hope the Minister would find this subamendment acceptable.
June 17, 1988

If I may, I will proceed to the second amendment. In the Senate's amendments, there is an amendment concerning the relationship of the process for dealing with refugee claims and the process for dealing with a perceived security risk. What the Senate proposed was that there be a section created which says that among those who will not be allowed to make the refugee claim is (A) described in paragraph 19(l)(c) or (B)(iii):
... a person described in paragraph 19(1 )(e), (f) or (g) or 27(1 )(c) or (2)(c), if the Minister is of the opinion that the application of sections 45 to 48 and 70 and 71 to that person would be contrary to the public interest;-
It is those last words I propose to change. My motion would read:
That the motion be amended in the proposed amendment to the Senate amendment No. 4 by deleting in subparagraph (iii) all the words after "(2)(c)".
That is to say: " ... if the Minister is of the opinion ..." The Minister has made a variation in the following words. Instead of saying "that the application of Sections 45 to 48 and 70 and 71", the Minister's amendment reads: "If the Minister is of the opinion that it would not be in the public interest to have the refugee claim determined under this Act". The Minister's words and the Senate's words have the same effect, but I am concerned with the ground upon which such a determination would be made. In Section 19(1 )(ii)(B) the ground for rejecting the claim depends on it being a person who the Minister has certified constitutes a danger to the public in Canada. I think that is a much more objective ground and, in that sense, a much more reasonable ground, upon which to base such an administrative decision. If the Minister has certified that a certain person is a danger to the public in Canada, there are limited provisions for having that decision reviewed by the Security Review Agency. There are some opportunities for the intervention of the normal procedures of justice such as habeas corpus and the right to counsel, even though the right to counsel is limited by the option of an in camera hearing from which counsel would be excluded. Nevertheless, the charge of being a danger to the public and the necessity of being able to show someone, such as a judge, the evidence of that danger, is a suitable limit on the power of either the Minister or the officials. It is the sort of limit that, for centuries, we have sought to develop and strengthen in our democracy.
Therefore, I believe the words used "who the Minister has certified constitutes a danger to the public in Canada" are acceptable words, but the words used in paragraph (iii) below: " ... if the Minister is of the opinion that to admit that person would be contrary to the public interest", is so undefined, so subjective and so general that I believe we should not allow that to creep into our law.
Parliamentary democracy in England became well established about three centuries ago when people decided they would not allow the King to use arbitrary power. They would not allow the King to just say, "I do not like him, so off with his head", or, "I do not like him, so kick him out of the
Immigration Act, 1976
country", or, "I do not like him, so remove him from office". There were military battles fought in England to establish the principle that even the King, or in this case the King's Minister or the Queen's Minister, must show some reason and not just use a blanket phrase such as "contrary to the public interest".
I believe that at the same time, three centuries ago, in France, the phrase used when the King was giving carte blanche to some servant to go and get rid of someone, was simply "reasons of state ". If the bearer has done what he has done through "reasons of state" then, of course, he is not to be accused or prosecuted even if he murdered someone. We rejected that three centuries ago. We did not want that in England and we do not want that in Canada.
Reasons of state or simply reasons of public interest are not good enough when a matter is very serious, and this is very serious. There could be a person with a legitimate refugee claim. He could also be a person who, because perhaps he came from a dictatorship such as Chile, was accused of having done subversive acts against the Government of General Pinochet. That is one of the causes referred to here. If he falls under certain clauses and the Minister says it would not be in the public interest to have his refugee claim processed, it could not be processed. What 1 am saying is that it is not enough for the Minister to say: "General Pinochet does not like him and neither do I". That is not in accordance with our democratic rules. It is also not in accordance with the UN convention with respect to the status of refugees which we signed 20 years ago and which the Government still boldly claims to support. If that person fell under the displeasure of General Pinochet or some other tyrant, he should be judged not according to whether the Minister does not like him, but according to whether it can be shown he is a danger to the public in Canada; not in Chile, not in Vietnam, not in the Soviet Union, not in Mozambique, not in South Africa, but in Canada.
This introduction of the phrase "the public interest" at this time is of particular concern because of a case that hit the newspapers a few weeks ago in which the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) was reported to have influenced the Minister and the Department of Immigration to exclude a Sikh refugee claimant by the name of Santokh Singh Bagga on the grounds that to allow him to make a refugee claim, to allow him to have his refugee claim heard, would be contrary to the public interest in Canada. In that case it was reported and never refuted that that person had received a security clearance from CSIS. It had been alleged by officials of the Government of India that they had no complaint against him. Yet the Minister, in correspondence with his colleague, the then Minister of Employment and Immigration, alleged that this person was wanted in India on suspicion of certain crimes. In other words, there was no agreement among our officials as to whether there was substance to the Minister's vague allusions. It was clear that, according to our existing law, the Minister had no right to ask that the opportunity of making a refugee claim and having it heard should be withheld from Santokh Singh Bagga.

Immigration Act, 1976
It appears that the object of this change would be to give the Minister the power that he then undertook to use-although he did not rightfully have such power, and I believe that matter may come before the courts but I have not heard that it has as yet-the power to finger any refugee claimant that he did not like and say it would be contrary to the public interest to let that person make a claim. I believe that would be a very undemocratic precedent to establish. It would not only damage the cases of certain refugee claimants but it would also undermine a fundamental principle of Canadian law that a person should not be hurt without being accused of something to which he could answer. In that case the Secretary of State was also quoted as complaining about the fact that Sikhs had been given refugee status in Canada.
It would appear that if the Secretary of State for External Affairs had this clause to use he might simply ban all Sikhs from making refugee claims in Canada. There might be others, perhaps the Bangladeshis, the Chileans or the people from Mozambique. We do not know, but if the Minister said, "I don't want any of those people making refugee claims", their stories would simply not be heard by the refugee process in Canada. That would be a very unfortunate law for Parliament to enact and it might very well be challenged in the courts.
My concern at present, however, is with the responsibility of Parliament. I am asking that the words in subparagraph (iii), "if the Minister is of the opinion that it would be contrary to the public interest to have that claim considered under our present law", be replaced by the words, "who the Minister has certified constitutes a danger to the public in Canada".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak once again on Bill C-55 and have one more chance to show my opposition to government policy that I believe betrays one of the oldest Canadian traditions, a tradition of welcome to people who have been persecuted or oppressed in another country. This tradition goes back to the earliest arrival of non-indigenous people in Canada. It goes back to the arrival of the Huguenots in New France. The United Empire Loyalists came to Canada fleeing from the excesses of the American dream. We have a history of receiving blacks fleeing from slavery in the United States and coming through the underground railroad. We have members of the historic peace churches, the Mennonites, the Doukhobors, the Hutterites who came to Canada, sometimes by a very circuitous route, to escape the enforced militarism of various European countries. They wanted a new way of thinking and did not want to be bound by old European ways of thinking which prescribed how everybody should think.
Since the Second World War we have had refugees from war-torn Europe and from behind the Iron Curtain. Over
400,000 of them have come to Canada since the Second World War. In the last few years we have seen a great many refugees coming from Southeast Asia. Particularly in recent times, because of our traditions, refugees have wanted to come to Canada from Latin America. Two years ago the Canadian people were awarded the Nansen Medal for receiving refugees from other parts of the world. But this is not the only tradition in Canada. There is a counter tradition, a tradition of ethno-centrism, of xenophobia, a fear of the stranger. That goes back to the roots of our human psyche for all of us, an intolerance of differences, a preference for the known and for the comfortable, which sometimes degenerates into bigotry.
As individuals, political Parties, societies and churches, I suppose we all share both traditions. We have on the one hand a tradition of openness and hospitality toward other people. On the other hand we have this bigotry and intolerance, which every so often crops up and sometimes dominates our lives and society. Every so often I find myself betrayed by something that comes up, some bigotry or intolerance within my own life that makes me ashamed when I recognize it later on.
The question we have to decide when we are making conscious policy decisions, when we sit down to make rational decisions about the direction in which our individual lives should go or the direction in which our nation should be going, is which tradition do we follow? Certainly when we look at the situation of people coming to Canada claiming refugee status we know there is a problem.
Speaking on this issue the Minister told us that some 60,000 people are now waiting to have their refugee determination status clarified. It is time there was some clarification. There have been royal commissions and committees of this House which have looked at this issue. Recommendations have been made which, if followed, would have resulted in clarification and a fair and speedier process, preventing the backlog from continuing to build up, a process to ensure that everyone would have a full hearing and the right to appeal. We do not have that in Bill C-55. We have a Bill that follows the tradition of fear and intolerance. That is why we are so opposed to it on this side of the House. In attempting to meet a real problem as we all recognize, it resorts to fear and intolerance, and there are measures in this Bill that will destroy the openness that we in Canada have come to see as a hallmark of our society. The tradition we wish to enshrine is one of openness and of welcome to refugees.
Carlos Fuentes in his book The Old Gringo said:
A muckraking reporter needs a robber baron as God needs Satan.
In the same way democratic socialists sometimes find it handy to have a right-wing ideologue as a convenient focus for our remarks. Sometimes we are even tempted to create straw men so that we can attack the straw men, but when it comes to Bill C-55 we do not create a straw man. We have a genuine
June 17, 1988

right-wing ideologue who has stated the policy very beautifully, I am referring to the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary. Last week, the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen), in response to a comment made by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon), said, as reported on page 16348 of Hansard:
The Member began, for example, by saying his forbear came here in 1S48 as a result of the failed revolutions in Germany. I understand that since my grandparents and great grandparents came from much the same kind of background.
However, he went on to say that the refugees today are the same as those in 1848, as if nothing has happened in the world since 1848 that would change the outlook or behavioural practices of people wanting to come to Canada.
Let me list just a few of the concepts which have now formed the behavioural patterns of people. For example, nihilism, which basically says it does not matter since nothing matters anyway. So you can do what you want. It is all a black future. There is no good consequence of anything, anyway, so go ahead and do what you want. There is existentialism, which makes everyone's individual outlook paramount. There is no uniform absolute. Nothing is clearly right or wrong.
Therefore, the expression of your own particular authenticity is the most moral thing you can do. There is no absolute morality so it does not matter if you incite violence or peace in its own self. That is a very popular concept.
There is dialectical materialism. It began to be popular around 1848 but was not pervasive at that time. But for the last 150 years witness eastern Europe and the effect of dialectical materialism, where the state is supreme and individual rights are nothing. They have value only to the extent and to the degree they support the state. How about situational ethics, again where nothing is right or wrong except the situation in which you happen to be. It depends on the situation.
Finally, the Marxist theology of Latin America which espouses violence for their cause. I want to remind the professor that when we have that cauldron of beliefs in the system, the thought forms of people coming to Canada have changed in the last 150 years, and Canada deserves some protection from people whose thought forms have changed, if they no longer hold to absolute rights and wrongs.
The key issue here, of course, is the Hon. Member's final statement. He said that people have changed in the last 150 years and that Canada deserves some protection from people whose thought forms have changed if they no longer hold to absolute rights and wrongs. I believe that we in Canada need protection from those whose thinking has not changed in the last 150 years, those who believe that their own way of interpreting right and wrong is the absolute law of the universe.
The Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta listed five different concepts that he felt were dangerous to Canada. I am not sure how he sees Bill C-55 preventing these concepts from coming into Canada. Some have already sneaked in over the border from the United States. Perhaps we have to do something to tighten up the free trade agreement a bit.
The Hon. Member talks about nihilism, existentialism, dialectical materialism, situational ethics and Marxist theology. We do not know how Bill C-55 will keep these things out, but the point is that the statement made by the Hon. Member gives some idea of the thinking of some Conservative Members, at least, as to the reason behind Bill C-55. It is to
Immigration Act, 1976
keep out people who do not think properly. It is a question of ideology rather than of refugee determination.
I know that the Hon. Member has never had a dialectical thought in his life, so I will not talk about dialectical materialism. I will not ask the Hon. Member to tempt himself with the thought of nihilism, to look into the abyss and see nothing there. Just this morning someone defined a nihilist as a Conservative who looks into the by-election opportunities in Lac-Saint-Jean, sees that there is nothing there and is tempted to despair. I will not ask the Hon. Member to be tempted by nihilism or dialectics, but I would like him to think existentially for a moment.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. This just underscores what I have felt for a long time. Israelites and Mennonites are about the same.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The Hon. Member is absolutely correct. The history of the Mennonites of being forced from one country to another and finally finding refuge in Canada is so important to this whole debate. The commandment that you shall not wrong a stranger or oppress him for you were strangers in the land of Egypt means that you shall not wrong a refugee for you were strangers in Russia or wherever. Many people have different traditions in their own families and their own faiths. If they look back, they will see where they were strangers or sojourners or refugees. It is that kind of existential thinking that I appeal to the Hon. Member and to all Hon. Members to use. Let us put ourselves in the position of the refugees and look at Bill C-55 from that point of view.
What happens when we look at Bill C-55 from the point of view of a refugee? Let us look at it, for example, from the point of view of a Salvadoran who has escaped from the persecution, the oppression, the war and the death squads that exist in that country. In spite of the farce of elections that took place a few years ago there and the facade of a democratic Government, right-wing oppression continues in that country. We can imagine this Salvadoran making his or her way to the United States and living a precarious underground existence, knowing very well that if discovered, he or she could be deported. In 1982, for example, out of 12,000 refugees, or people who claimed refugee status in the United States, only 26 were accepted. The United States is not very hospitable towards Salvadorans. In the last year the United States has passed legislation which imposes very severe penalties upon anyone who gives employment or harbours illegal refugees.
Therefore, these people have a very precarious role in the United States and find their way to Canada. Once Bill C-55 is in place, instead of being able to come to Canada and have a full hearing they will be subject to a prescreening process. If it is determined that they came from the United States, there is a very good chance that the United States will be declared a safe third country to which they can be sent back. There is no guarantee.
The Library of Parliament studied this issue with regard to the safe third country, and said:
Even when the wording of the provision is finally settled, it will probably still be very difficult to enumerate or explain the factors that will underlie the safe country list or how those factors will operate in any given case. For example, what are the implications if the general human rights record of a country is a criterion? It is not immediately apparent how human rights would be relevant. Some countries have a general record that is good (or reasonably so) for the majority of their citizens, but poor in respect of certain sectors of the population. Turkey is a case in point-
Similarly, the general human rights record of a country in relation to all their own nationals might be excellent. The countries of Western Europe come to mind.
Yet, in the special case of non-nationals who happen to be refugees or refugee claimants, the attitude may be quite different. Again, certain incidents in Europe in the last five years will serve as examples of this. Yet the criterion of the human rights record would imply that all of those countries should be placed on the list.
The foregoing discussion illustrates the difficulties in establishing what a safe country is, in particular by referring to its general human rights record. If that is to be a criterion (a point not yet established at time of writing) its application may prove very difficult.
Especially in view of the difficulties just discussed relating to general human rights, a country's record on refoulement will, and should, be the factor most central to a safe country designation, yet how will that be assessed?
If individual examples of refoulement (probably indirect, but refoulement nevertheless) in relation to a country were sufficient to keep that country off the list, very few countries, even in Western Europe, would qualify.
We have again problems with what is going to happen. We have the concept of sending people back to a so-called safe third country, but what do we mean by that?
The Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) has pointed out the bias in Canadian policy. I am not sure whether it is as a result of bias or just of mistake that this morning's headline in The Globe and Mail talks about a Mozambican terrorist who has been granted refugee status in Canada even though he was not on the United Nations High Commission for Refugees list of refugees. It appears that the appropriate consultation was not taken, there was not a CSIS clearance, yet this person has been granted refugee status in Canada. On the other hand, a Sikh, a non-violent person, has been denied refugee status by the direct intervention of the Minister.
The Inter-Church Committee for Refugees has written, again underlining the need for legislation which would provide access for all claimants to a full, fair, and independent hearing and a meaningful appeal. They say:
Legislation which compromises the level of justice accorded to refugees is unnecessary and should be resisted.
It is on that basis that we are resisting Bill C-55. It is not in accordance with the best Canadian traditions of openness and hospitality. It does a disservice to Canada and a disservice to refugees.

Mr. Speaker, on Sunday, June 19, the Board of Parks and Recreation of the City of Vancouver will be celebrating a century of service and marking the 100th anniversary of Stanley Park.
The first resolution of the First City Council of Vancouver petitioned the then Dominion Government to grant what was at the time a government military reserve to the city for a public park. Ottawa consented to lease the park to the city for 99 years, and Lord Stanley of Preston, then Governor General of Canada, gave his name to the park with these memorable words: "To the use and enjoyment of people of all colours, creeds and customs for all time, I name thee Stanley Park".
You and I know, Mr. Speaker, that Stanley Park is famous for its many features, from the zoo and the aquarium, to Lumbermen's Arch, Pauline Johnson's Memorial, the beautiful totem poles and, of course, the Lord Stanley Monument. But it is the park itself, an island of green shining like an emerald jewel in the middle of a large urban setting, which is the major attraction for tourists and citizens alike.
The fact that Stanley Park has retained much of its original natural and uncluttered beauty is a tribute to the people of Vancouver who have been vigilant over the years in their efforts to protect the park from overdevelopment and from commercialization.
I am sure I speak on your behalf as well, as a neighbouring Member of Parliament, Mr. Speaker, when 1 say that all of our constituents in Vancouver Quadra, Vancouver South, and other constituencies of Vancouver join me in congratulating the Vancouver Parks Board on its role in preserving Stanley Park over the last century and for future generations.

PRESERVATION OF ROUGE VALLEY WILDERNESS AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Ontario Government must be convinced to designate the Rouge Valley System as a recreational park or to participate with the federal Government and make it a Canadian heritage park.
This is a unique wilderness area of over 5,000 acres stretching north to Markham and to the Bruce's Mill conservation area. It is rich in natural and historic resources. It contains the largest forest in the Greater Metro area and numerous species of plant, fish, bird and animal life.
The Rouge Valley is also equally rich in our cultural legacy with archeological remains of Indian settlements dating back thousands of years, along with the earliest evidence of European settlements.
We must protect the Rouge Valley System from becoming the exclusive domain of a luxury housing development, or even worse, a dump, as has been threatened.
With the world's environment at a crossroads and with the public's unprecedented support for natural heritage preservation, let us take a leadership role to protect the Rouge Valley System.

SEVENTY-NINTH OBSERVANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Sunday, June 19, Canadians will observe Father's Day. Young children will deluge their fathers with hand-made cards, and hand-picked ties and socks. Older children will reflect on intimate childhood remembrances.
Father's Day observances appeared in several North American locations in the early 1900s. But the idea is generally credited to Sonora Louise Smart Dodd of Spokane, Washington.
In 1909, inspired by her own father, Mrs. Dodd suggested to her church pastor that a special day be set aside to honour all fathers.
Through the intervening years the Father's Day idea has been officially approved by one U.S. President; turned down by two; thrown out by the U.S. House of Representatives on two occasions; and abandoned by the City of Chicago. Against these odds, however, Father's Day survives.
In 1988, 79 years after its first observance, Father's Day is officially celebrated in 20 countries as the one special day of the year when children honour their fathers for their loving care and devotion to their families.
May I wish all Canadian fathers a very happy Father's Day-especially my own Dad.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. As the Secretary of State knows, the Secretary-General of the United Nations is in the process of arranging a meeting in Geneva next month to try to bring about a solution to the problems in Cyprus.
Two of the key issues in those negotiations will be the guarantee of minority rights and also the possibility of setting up a federal system of government. Canada has had a peacekeeping force in Cyprus since 1963. We have had a lot of experience with minority rights in this country and with a federal system of government. We have an international reputation as a peacekeeper yet we have always played a passive as opposed to an active role in these negotiations.
Will the Secretary of State for External Affairs give the House his undertaking that Canada will play a very active as opposed to a passive role in these upcoming negotiations with a view to bringing about a solution of the problems in Cyprus?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question and his interest in a matter that is of great importance to Canadians, not simply because of the presence of our troops in Cyprus in a peacekeeping role.
We are encouraged by the interest being taken by the Secretary-General of the United Nations. Certainly the Hon. Member would want the Government of Canada to support those measures fully and not to do things that might detract from the initiative of the Secretary-General. We will support his initiatives fully. If there is something more that we can do in the view of the Secretary-General that will contribute to a peaceful solution of a long-standing situation in Cyprus, then we certainly will co-operate fully with the Secretary-General of the United Nations with that in view.
The Hon. Member will know that every six months the question arises as to whether we should renew our presence of troops in the area. We have decided to do that. Last year we increased our commitment.
It would be in everyone's interest if Canada could contribute to a solution that would resolve the fundamental problem. We are very much interested in doing that in collaboration with the Secretary-General of the UN.

subsubtopic: DELAY IN GOVERNMENT RESPONSE TO COMMITTEE REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order to bring to the attention of the House a breach of the Standing Orders. Standing Order 99(2) reads as follows:
Within 150 days of the presentation of a report from a standing or special
committee, the government shall, upon the request of the committee, table a
comprehensive response thereto.
On January 19 of this year the Standing Committee on Environment and Forestry presented a report on the storage and disposal of high-level radioactive waste. The title of the report is The Eleventh Hour. It contains 15 recommendations that deal with the nuclear fuel cycle. It is an important, in fact critical, report. I repeat that it was presented on January 19.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) who asked me to raise this point in her absence today, has been informed by the clerk of the committee that today represents the 150th day that has passed since the presentation of this report.
At the time the report was presented the committee requested a government response. The arrangement for such a request was an innovation under parliamentary reform which was intended to upgrade and reinforce the real influence of parliamentary committees.
We in this Party participated actively in the parliamentary reform process. We believe in parliamentary reform and believe in operating within the rules of this House of Commons, unlike the Government which has no hesitation in suspending and throwing out the rules at the slightest opportunity.
June 17, 1988

The Government has not responded to the standing committee's report within the 150-day deadline. It has, therefore, breached Standing Order 99(2).

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: POINT OF ORDER
subsubtopic: DELAY IN GOVERNMENT RESPONSE TO COMMITTEE REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 think this is a valid point of order. The rules provide for no exceptions. Where a response is requested by a committee to its report the Government must table the response in 150 days. There is no doubt that this is the last day for filing such a report within the rules.
We are talking here about the first report of the Standing Committee on Environment and Forestry entitled High-Level Radioactive Waste in Canada: The Eleventh Hour. Quite apart from the rules, this report should have an early response because of its importance. I regret to say that one can only wonder why the Government has not been able to table such a response in view of the importance of the subject matter of the committee report.
Equally serious is the seeming unwillingness of the Government to live within the rules. These are rules which I have often characterized not only as part of parliamentary reform but rules for which the Government takes credit for that reason.
We are dealing with an effort by the Government to suspend the rules, but at least in that case, which we do not accept, the Government is waiting until the House agrees, if it ever happens, to a motion to suspend the rules and do something other than is what is provided for in the rules. Here, with respect to the failure to file a response to the report of the Standing Committee on Environment and Forestry, the Government is simply ignoring the rules, not even seeking and obtaining the agreement of the House in an effort to do something for which the rules do not provide. I regret very much that 1 have to bring to your attention this breach of the rules. I hope the Government will realize that it has the same obligation to live within the rules, unless and until they are properly changed. It has not done so. This is another deplorable act by the Government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of State and Minister of State (Treasury Board)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
subtopic: POINT OF ORDER
subsubtopic: DELAY IN GOVERNMENT RESPONSE TO COMMITTEE REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if one were to examine the record 1 think one would find that in almost all cases the Government has met the deadline of 150 days. I am advised that this report is in the final throes of preparation and that it should be tabled in the House shortly.
At all times we have tried to meet this requirement. Unfortunately, due to the complexity of this report, we were unable to meet the requirements of the rules. I assure my hon. friend that it was not a wilful matter. It was simply that we wanted to get the best reply possible to a very comprehensive committee report. Therefore, I submit that it is correct that we are in breach of the rules, but I think it is the exception rather than the rule and I can assure the House that it will be tabled shortly.

There is a tradition of openness and of welcome to strangers and to refugees, and another tradition which, unfortunately, we share to some extent, of being more fearful and closed toward people with differences.
I highlighted the comments of the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) in the debate last week wherein he talked about the need to protect Canada against people who had certain ways of thinking that had

June 17, 1988

arisen in the last 150 years and with whom he did not happen to agree.
I talked about the lack of access in Bill C-55 to a full hearing before a person is denied refugee status. I talked about the lack of an appeal process. I talked about the fact that we still have this possibility of sending someone back to a third country, and yet we do not have any real guarantee that he or she will receive adequate treatment in that third country.
The Elon. Member for Gatineau talked about real refugees as being those who are in refugee camps somewhere else in the world and that that is where Canada should obtain its refugees from. The fact is that refugees do not originate in refugee camps. They appeal to some country for refugee status and are placed in camps. Canada in the past has often been able to pick and choose which refugees we wish to accept. But there have always been two streams of refugees who would come to Canada. There were those who would be in refugee camps where we would go and select certain refugees who had come to Canada. There were those who themselves would come and appear on our front doorstep as it were, claiming refugee status.
This is where the problem has been, when a number of people have claimed refugee status, some of them being bogus claimants, and we did not have an adequate system for dealing with that. Thus we have built up a backlog of people who are claimants for refugee status, some legitimate and a great many of whom we all admit are not legitimate.
What the Government has done over the last number of years, beginning with the Liberal Government, has been inadequate to deal with this situation. The Liberal Government appointed a royal commission under Rabbi Plaut to investigate this matter. He brought in a very good report in 1985. When the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration studied the report it brought in another report that contained some very good recommendations. They would have resulted in a much shorter, more expeditious process, but it would still have been a fair process for refugee claimants, a process which would have given them full access to a hearing within Canada. They would also have a fair appeal process.
The Government did not choose to act on that report. Instead, it brought in Bill C-55 which, as I pointed out earlier, does not have access to a full impartial hearing by a refugee determination board. It does not have any possibility of an adequate appeal. It is on that basis that the Government is really closing down this second stream of refugees so that it will be very difficult for people, particularly from Latin America, to come to Canada and claim refugee status. The great majority of refugees who come and present themselves to Canada asking for asylum come from Central and South America. I refer to legitimate refugees. We have had some bogus refugee claimants who have flown in here from other parts of the world. That issue needs to be addressed.
In trying to address that situation we have practically shut off this second stream of refugees. As the Hon. Member said, we should be getting all our refugees from refugee camps. That is one stream of refugees, but we still have to retain the openness of Canada to people who come to our doorstep asking for refugee asylum.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to rise in this debate on Bill C-55 in order to speak with my colleagues in support of an amendment to the Bill as it has come back from the other place, and amendments from my colleague, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), as well, which are very limited attempts in a Bill that is so bad in many sections. They are worthy attempts to try to restore something of the humanity that is required in our refugee legislation.
I note that the Parliamentary Secretary is present in the House. I trust that he will be with us a little while longer. I, too, would like to say something about the debate that took place here last Lriday in which he articulated some thoughts about the kind of supervision that we should be providing at the borders in order to be sure that we did not bring into the country and find settled among us as neighbours and eventually as fellow Canadians persons who might have one dangerous notion or another.
There was an exchange of views. In particular I am thinking of the response of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Essex- Windsor (Mr. Langdon), in which he suggested that what the Parliamentary Secretary was really suggesting would require thought police sitting at the borders looking for traces of nihilism, existentialism, particularly Christian existentialism, and persons who believe in dialectical materialism, and so on. That was a fair comment. It was a most appropriate response by my colleague to the suggestions of the Parliamentary Secretary.
I trust that he is listening since he has stepped out of the Chamber. I do not want to transgress the rules. However, I hope most devoutly that I have his ear since he and I are both, as it happens, of Mennonite origin. We happen neither of us to find our homes in Mennonite churches these days, having made other choices, as we are free to do in Canada. However, I confirmed with him earlier this day that his ancestors had come to Canada during the 1870s. His spouse's ancestors had come in before the Great War, around the turn of the century. That may perhaps give him a less keen appreciation of exactly what he was pointing to in his suggestions about people's ideas.
As I told him, I happen to combine the two traditions among Mennonites in Canada. My mother's ancestors, too, arrived in the migration to Manitoba in the 1870s. There, they faced the rigors of pioneering in the southern part of that province. My father's ancestry is that of the 1920s migration to Canada, refugees from Soviet Russia who were very happy to have escaped the Bolshevik revolution and what followed from it. They escaped with their lives although they were affected in health by the rigors of those years.

June 17, 1988

The fact of the matter is that it was a near thing that they got to Canada because, following the Great War of 1914-18, there was in Canada a fair amount of aversion to Mennonites. After all, they have a belief in conscientious objection. They do not want to participate in war. They seek alternatives to service in the army, navy and air force. That particular principle, the aversion to taking part in war and joining in the war effort against the empires of central Europe, aroused a great deal of reaction among neighbours of the Mennonites in Canada. It aroused a reaction which reached such a pitch that the Government of Canada decided to exclude Mennonites from migration to this country.
In the 1920s a new Government came to power after the unionist Government was defeated in 1921. The new Government happened to be Liberal and, to its credit, it recognized the need for agricultural settlers. It was busy settling the veterans and the soldiers who were returning from the front, but it also saw the need for other farmers. That Government decided to allow Mennonites to migrate, but it imposed a restriction which affected the life of more than one young Mennonite man for all his lifetime, and that was very much my father's experience.
The Mennonites who came to Canada in the 1920s were required to stay on the land. For many of them that might have been quite a satisfactory restriction of experience, and they may have been quite content to farm as their ancestors had done in the Ukraine, in East Prussia, and all the way back to Friesland. For others that was not something that was easily accepted. I know that my father would have preferred to have been an engineer, or work with machinery. In fact, after almost 30 years of farming in southern Manitoba he sold his farm and bought a welding shop in the Town of Carmen. He spent the last four or five years of his working life blissfully happy, overworked, and not charging enough for his labours, I am quite certain, but blissfully happy working with machinery and helping farmers with the repair of their machinery, and other welding work.
From the 1920s, the prejudices of the Great War, through to the experience of one Mennonite Canadian in the 1960s and 1970s we have the consequences of prejudice expressed in the law of Canada, the regulations, and the requirements laid on Canadians. I do not know if this particular requirement was legislated or made a regulation. The fact that the Government had made this a condition of the return to migration was sufficient for most of the Mennonites. They are honourable people, and if that was the commitment that they had given, then that was what they were going to do in Canada, or at least they would do so for 30 or 40 years and perhaps eventually, when there was no possibility of the farm being continued in the family, like my father, decided to do something else.
I use this particular experience at some length to illustrate to the Parliamentary Secretary that to suggest dangerous notions is something that he should be profoundly uneasy
Immigration Act, 1976
about doing. If his ancestors did not face that type of prejudice on the part of fellow Canadians, others of his ethnocultural community did. He should certainly know better than to suggest that Canada wants to put thought police at the borders to check people out to ensure that they will not be a danger to the country.
In this context, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has served up similar fears to us in the last month in reaction to another community in Canada, the Canadian Sikh community. I wish to say very carefully on that particular point that to have the law enforcement agencies of Canada ensuring that the law is not broken, to ensure by one means or another that Canadians are not involved in support of violence in Canada or elsewhere and that those who participate in violence are punished, are all necessary things for the appropriate agencies of the Canadian Government to carry out.
But to suggest that because someone has lived with terrible experiences or lived in terrible situations and has come to a certain view of the world, and that that person should not have the right to come to Canada or should be stopped from coming into this country, because presumably those ideas are so ingrained that they will continue to work in that person's mind and make him a threat to this country, is surely to misunderstand the psychology of practically all persons. It is to miss the key point that people are driven to desperate views of the world, to desperate measures by circumstances in which they see no other way of dealing with it.
In this country we provide constitutional means. We allow freedom of assembly. We allow freedom of speech. We expect persons to use those means to express their viewpoints. We are opposed to ostracizing any group. We are profoundly opposed in law to guilt by association. We want to allow people the opportunity to seek the objectives that they are prepared to state with clear face, without having to blush or be embarrassed about their goals. I mean by that goals that can be stated in a meeting without embarrassment. They should be able to pursue those goals by legitimate means, and we are not involved in questioning the thoughts or philosophies involved here.
I am sorry that I do not have the opportunity to ask my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly), who is, after all, an ordained minister of the Church of Canada, whether he had some further thoughts. He cited the Old Testament to splendid purpose in supporting the necessity to offer refuge to those in danger of life and limb. I would have liked to ask him what his further observations were on the attitude of someone who thinks that ideas must be kept out, and presumably that means keeping out persons who may hold these ideas, and that we might as a consequence see lives sacrificed. We might see a person suffering loss of limb or loss of life, as is all too possible in country after country these days, simply because we are suspicious of the ideas held by some persons or perhaps even political Parties in that country that they have come to in desperate response to the terrible circumstances imposed on them.

June 17, 1988

Perhaps the Parliamentary Secretary will respond to those observations. I expect he is with us in ear as well as in spirit. He may have some observations of his own on the suggestion that it is bad ideas that we will keep out without regard to the persons who happen to hold those ideas, and that somehow human life, which I have no doubt he would hold very sacred, would be maimed or lost because he is preoccupied with ideology. That tells us a good deal about attitudes that are behind the Government's Bill.
Perhaps you will remember, Madam Speaker, that about 17 months ago I had to say something in the House that was not pleasant and which aroused a certain amount of reaction when the then Minister for Employment and Immigration made a free-time speech on television in the Province of Quebec in which he was celebrating his own area, very close to where the by-election is currently under way, and he spoke of a region in which people are rather untouched by immigration and some of the other world realities. I suppose there is some truth to that, perhaps there is a great deal of truth to that. I do not think it is the total truth for the Lac St. Jean-Saguenay region of the Province of Quebec. No part of the country is free of persons from other continents of this world who have come to find refuge. I know there are multicultural organizations in that area to which the Minister might have been sensitive.
When the Minister went on to talk about an area that was demographically pure in population he aroused terrible fears in many people. I know very definitely that for members of Canada's Jewish community these were reminders of what had been said in the Nuremberg trials. What is most distressing is that requests from the Canadian Jewish Congress to withdraw those statements were not acted upon. I do not know what was in the Minister's mind in refusing to do so, but the fact that he insisted on standing by those statements for some reason of lack of support for any withdrawal on the part of his colleagues in the Quebec caucus of the Conservative Party, I find quite troubling, as I expect you would also, Madam Speaker, as someone who is very well acquainted with many members of that caucus.
The possibility of racism in Canada, supported and expressed in legislation such as this, is something people of many backgrounds across this country find intensely troubling. The woman who is now Minister for Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) cannot say that the constituency she represents in Metropolitan Toronto is free of the knowledge of the diversity of our country and the needs of people who are in danger of life and limb in other parts of the world. That makes it all the more distressing that she can become Minister, carry these Bills, and refuse to take up with her colleagues significant changes. Her comments in presenting the Bill are found in Hansard of June 3, 1988, page 16095. She said:
These two vital Bills, which I consider a complementary package, have been considered from every possible angle by parliamentarians, non-governmental organizations, legal experts, the media and many others. As a Government, we have encouraged the scrutiny and appreciate the efforts and sincere concerns of those who have contributed to the examination of these Bills.
She does not say that practically every person who appeared and practically every organization which made a representation to the committee-and I have this on the authority of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Spadina-and he can correct me if I am exaggerating-was opposed to this Bill. Practically every presentation was profoundly critical of what the Government was doing. How can one, in all honour and with any kind of integrity, say the words I have just read and not recognize that this process of consultation was profoundly critical of the legislation and called for fundamental changes which the Government has refused to carry through? How is it possible for an honourable Minister to do that?
We have lost a great deal in time and we have suffered damage in the attitudes of Canadians by reason of what the Government has done. The Government promised a campaign against racism in the fall of 1986. One would expect that sometime in 1987 it would be accomplished. But instead of such a campaign being undertaken, there was a whipping up of feeling, after a ship of Sikh refugee claimants landed on the Nova Scotia coast. The Canadian Government whipped up that feeling and there were incredible responses. I lived in astonishment and distress for days having heard what the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) said in apparent acceptance of the Government's suggestion that these people should be sent away. It took days before he changed his stance. Such a yielding to racism in this country, may I say with care, is not surprising coming from someone who represents a Vancouver riding, because on the West Coast these feelings of concern about Asians coming to Canada have existed for a long, long time. I am sure the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition would eschew any such motive in himself, but that was just one demonstration of the effect of the Government's actions.
We have seen more than a year pass without anything like a campaign against racism. The present Minister for Multicul-turalism promised, trying for some support for the Government in the context of the upcoming election, whenever it happens to be, more money for multiculturalism, and a good chunk of that money, a couple of million dollars, perhaps, will be put into the area of work on race relations. This Government shamefully neglected race relations for most of the time from September 17, 1984. It left a couple of people in the area, but there was no program, no strategy, no resources to do anything. Now when the next election draws near, after the Government has done its damage with this legislation, it will belatedly spend some money in this area to try, if it can, to rescue things. It is terribly late to do that.
All those persons across the country who recognize what the Government is doing with Bill C-55 and Bill C-84, and who have been hoping that at some point the presentations by all those groups, by churches and by those concerned about
June 17, 1988

refugees from wherever they may come, those persons who want to work in the Canadian tradition that brought us the Nansen Medal, those who have been waiting for some evidence that the Government has changed its mind, will not be impressed by more spending on race relations. They want real action in which this Government will arrest the feelings of racism that exist in the country and return it to the traditions of openness about which my colleagues, the Hon. Member for Spadina and the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly), have already spoken so very well earlier this day.

Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for her question. This is the sort of thing that should never be done easily or loosely. It always deserves to be done carefully. I speak, of course, from my background as a teacher of Canadian history, Associate Professor of History at Lakehead University, on political leave, and also as someone who has lived and taught in the interior of British Columbia. I want to be very careful because the feelings of prejudice and racism have existed in many parts of Canada. I respect the desire of my colleague from southern Ontario not to have anything said unfairly. I think the fact remains, perhaps because British Columbians live across the Pacific from Asia and because Japanese immigrants and, before that, Chinese workers who built the railway, settled there, may have had more experience with Asians on the Pacific coast. I think of a man who was one of British Columbia's Lieutenant Governors, James Dunsmuir, whose family owned large coal mines on Vancouver Island. The Dunsmuirs were capable of bringing in labour that could be discriminated against, as in law one could in British Columbia. They used that labour to break strikes by British-born workers in those communities, and that, of course, built up terrible feelings of resentment. So there are these factors in the history of the province to be noted.
If there is any question about the validity of suggesting that British Columbia may be more racist, it would surely be seen in the laws of the province that apply to citizenship and voting rights and so on. After all, these were laws that, for a long time, were left to the provinces to establish. The Canadian Government has not always filled areas of its own jurisdiction very well, and in matters of voting, when a province discriminated deliberately against Asians, denying them voting rights and citizenship, in those professions where one could not enter unless one were a citizen able to vote, this exclusion actually closed doors. This was discrimination in law, British Columbia style.

The last thing anyone wants in these areas is to have any possibility of having an attitude of being holier than thou. I think one can quite fairly recognize in British Columbia's history the whipping up of feeling against Japanese Canadians particularly that led eventually to the action in 1942 of uprooting a community, seizing property, selling it off for whatever and relocating people into detention and work camps et cetera. Japanese Canadian redress is one of the final expressions of the racism that prevailed in B.C. to which a Canadian Government tragically yielded in the midst of war, or which, in retrospect, we would surely say was against racism, first of all the racism of the Nazi system.

I think it is probably a fact that people are most intolerant of those next to them.
I was brought up in a situation where there were no blacks. 1 never learned to be intolerant of blacks. There were very few Asians on the Prairies where I grew up. I did not have that kind of prejudice. We tend to have prejudices built into us when we are face to face with a situation. I think what the Hon. -either prejudice against other persons whether they be on the basis of race, creed, religion, colour, gender, et cetera. Many of the people in this Chamber probably face potential racism themselves whether they be Francophones working in an Anglophone atmosphere, women working in a predominately male atmosphere or men working in a predominately female atmosphere. For us to tackle the problem of racism, we have to look within ourselves.
I say that because by looking within ourselves we have to look at the content of this legislation before us today. In particular, in dealing with Bills C-55 and C-84 it is pretty clear that the Government has responded to concerns in a racist way. We recall that last summer there was supposed to have been an emergency going on because a couple of hundred refugees were seeking solace and refuge on our shores.
June 17, 1988

I think many people had hoped that there would be some fundamental changes to Bill C-55 and Bill C-84 when the Hon. Member for St. Paul's (Mrs. McDougall) took over the portfolio of Employment and Immigration. I thought she would return with legislation which would exclude the possibility of turning a boat away. I would have thought that she would have done that because in a period of war this country, not Vancouver, not Toronto, not a specific community, responded in a racist way by turning away a ship full of Jewish refugees who were seeking solace here. Eventually that ship was sent back and those people went to their deaths. That is a tragedy that should hang on the consciences of all Canadians, because that decision was made by a Government representing the people of Canada. We have made mistakes, and that one was a deadly and racist mistake that resulted in sending people to their deaths.
Why should we today, through a new piece of legislation, grant future Ministers the right to commit the same deadly errors that were committed in the past? Unless amendments are accepted, the Minister will actually be able to give responsibility for such a decision to someone else. A Minister or even a civil servant would be able to decide, on behalf of the people of Canada, to turn away a ship full of people.
I do not think anyone is suggesting that owners of ships who trade in human flesh and are trying to milk desperate people for hundreds and even thousands of dollars should not be dealt with, but surely the best way to achieve the dual objectives of opening the arms of our country to refugees and at the same time making sure that those who exploit them are dealt with in a severe fashion is a different way than the one proposed by this Bill. We can do it in a better and more humane way.
We can achieve those goals by permitting those who arrive on a boat to land in the same way as any other refugee. At the same time, we can bring in legislation which permits the seizure and sale of ships so that those who actually try to trade in human flesh will realize that they cannot sell passage to desperate people and walk away from it.
The owner of the ship that came in last summer walked away with hundreds of thousands of dollars. He was never dealt with. If we had seized that ship, fined the owner, and perhaps imprisoned him, that would have been the right way to deal with the culprit without victimizing the victims who are genuine refugees or, at the very least, people who have the right to be heard. These people had the right to plead their case without having a political decision being made by a Minister responding to the hot political climate of that particular summer. There should not have been a sudden determination that anyone who comes to this country of a different colour or race might not be desirable and therefore may be sent back.
I do not think we want to repeat the racist mistakes that Canada made in the past and for which we are all responsible. If we pass this legislation as it is currently written, we will be
Immigration Act, 1976
conferring on future Governments the ability to commit the same deadly errors that were committed when we sent a boatload of Jewish refugees to their deaths during war. I do not think we want to do that.
I do not think the Government has thought through the impact of the legislation it is asking Canadians to accept. All Canadians are proud of the fact that Canada is the only country that has actually been awarded international recognition for our contribution to the resettlement of refugees from Vietnam. Individuals have been recognized over the years, but Canada is the only country to have been awarded such international recognition.
With these two pieces of legislation we will destroy, in one fell swoop, Canada's reputation as a country with a humane policy toward people who are desperate, people who are without a homeland, people who are so desperate that they will pay someone thousands of dollars to get on a ship that may lead to nowhere. These people could be put on a life-raft out in the middle of the ocean, but they are so desperate because they are homeless and stateless that they are willing to take that chance. As a native born Canadian, I cannot even conceive of the desperation that I would feel if I would have to pack up my family-

The Hon. Member says that if I sit on that side I will know what desperation feels like. I can understand how he feels, given the potential results on Monday.
I cannot imagine how desperate some people must be that they would pack up their families, pay thousands of dollars to someone who at the very least has a questionable business background, and head off on a boat going God knows where, maybe nowhere, potentially to their deaths. Yet we are being asked to pass legislation which will tell those people that they will not even be given a fair hearing in this country. That is one provision of the Bill which absolutely must be changed.
The second area of concern deals with the safe third country concept. Because the Government does not wish to give potential refugees the opportunity to have their cases heard in our country, they will be sent to a third country.
The Government believes that the list of safe third countries should be drawn up by a committee which ultimately reports to the Minister. First, I would suggest that the safe third country concept is not a functional concept in the turbulent political time in which Canada finds itself in relation to other countries. Let us take the United States, as an example.
Most of us would consider the United States a safe country. However, is it safe for a refugee who comes from Central America, lands in Canada, and is then sent to the United States? Do we have any kind of guarantee that the United States will not send that person back to a place like El Salvador where he may in fact be facing certain death, or to a

June 17, 1988
*
Immigration Act, 1976
place like Chile where people have disappeared by the thousands? What kind of a guarantee do we have that in the turbulent political climate in the Americas, a safe third country concept should include the United States?
If it were left up to the Minister, with the so-called advisory committee, the Minister would be under a tremendous amount of political pressure to include the United States as one of the safe countries. We have a renewed, terrific relationship with the United States of America. Imagine what kind of a backlash there would be if we issued a list of safe third countries for refugees from Central America and the United States was absent from that list. Imagine what kind of pressure we would have from people like George Shultz and the President of the United States.
I do not think it is viable to suggest that the Minister who is subject to those kinds of political pressures should decide something like this about an issue we have tried to depoliticize. I do not think we want to place upon the Minister the responsibility for determining these so-called safe third countries. We would be setting a dangerous precedent. In very many instances what is a safe country to a Canadian is not necessarily a safe country to a potential refugee. That is another reason that this legislation, as it is currently drafted, is simply unworkable. The safe third country concept does not work. If the Minister is given the power to determine what constitutes a safe third country, the question will be a political one rather than a moral one.
The third area of the legislation which was not changed and with which we can absolutely not agree is that dealing with the Government's intention to provide an exclusion for a person who is "contrary to the public interest".
In other words, a refugee coming to this country can make application and say "I am a bona fide refugee; I have come to this country with nothing but the shirt on my back, my children, and my husband" or "my wife". The refugee determination process is set in motion and the refugee board can determine, after all the appropriate security checks, et cetera, that in fact the person is a bona fide refugee. Yet, the Government is reserving the right for an amendment for the exclusion of a person who is "contrary to the public interest".
It seems to me that that is exactly the kind of exception that we want to avoid. We have seen the case most recently of Santokh Singh. Indeed, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) may be called to report before the House because he refuses to appear before the committee and clear up the discrepancy of the refugee determination process as it relates to Santokh Singh.
Your Honour will recall that Mr. Singh went through the process. He in fact was cleared by the security people; he got clearance from CSIS as well as the general clearance carried out by the RCMP. He was also cleared by the refugee determination process. Then, all of a sudden, a foreign
Government, which happened to disagree fundamentally with the political views of a minority in its own community, allegedly contacted the Minister and said that this person should not be allowed into Canada because it was not in the public interest.
Even though the refugee determination process, in an independent fashion, had given clearance to this individual, by virtue of a foreign Government calling and saying that the person was not to be allowed in because he was "contrary to the public interests", the person can be sent away.
There are constituents in my own constituency of Hamilton East from the Ukraine who may not be the most beloved former citizens of their own country from which they were forced to flee and which Was taken over by the U.S.S.R. According to the amendment in this legislation the Soviet Government could call up and say "I don't think Zenon Kramer should be allowed into your country because he might be working contrary to the public interest". I am sure that Ivan Boyko, the current President of the National Congress of the Ukrainian Canadians, is not working in the public interest of the Government of the Soviet Union.
Do we think that by bringing in a Bill which permits the Minister to override the independent findings of a refugee board and respond to the alleged concerns of foreign Governments we will be able to maintain the independence* depoliticization, and integrity of the refugee determination process?
We do not think that is possible. That is why we cannot support the concept of an overriding amendment which would allow any Minister, if the political climate gets hot, notwithstanding what the refugee board may have determined or the security clearance of CSIS and the RCMP may have determined, to reserve the right to get rid of a person if a foreign Government calls up and says that we should. The Minister would be able to disregard the due process which has been the hallmark of the refugee determination process in Canada.
There are certainly three major concerns, some with which I have dealt. One is the safe third country concept. The weak appeal process is also of extreme concern. People who come to Canada to make refugee applications have approximately 72 hours in which to apprise themselves of the fact that they may be able to appeal the case. That was, in fact, extended from the original plan of 24 hours. In three days they may not be able to have access to counsel. They may not learn what opportunities they may have to appeal a decision of the Government. In fact, it seems to me that it is a fundamental flaw in the Bill to give them such a short pre-screening period and immediately to ship them out to the so-called safe third country. I am very surprised-

I am quite disappointed, after more than 30 years of progress by the Canadian Government on human rights and refugee policy in Canada, that on the matter of Japanese Canadians that was just mentioned, all Canadians should be

ashamed of what our Government has done. Madam Speaker, because my own daughter has a Japanese grandmother, according to the rules that were in effect during the Second World War, she could have been put in a prison camp by the Canadian Government. I think it is a disgrace for all Canadians that during the war, we reacted so strongly that we put bona fide Canadian citizens in prisons and concentration camps, just because they had a Japanese great-grandfather. They were put in a concentration camp for that. I do not want us to adopt retrograde policies that would allow us to turn back a ship. I think that the Bill as it stands is a step back, and Canadians and Members of the House should reject it.
