Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate. This is not the first time I have spoken on this legislation in the House, but it is necessary to keep debating it until the Government gets the message.
Immigration Act, 1976
I was asking my colleague why the Government has brought Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, into this House. The legislation has been widely condemned. I conclude that the Government has brought in this legislation because it has been playing to the fear that people have about false refugee claimants and immigrants. It has been appealing to the mass audience in trying to score political points. That was evidenced by the fact that Parliament was called back into emergency session last summer to deal with the question of immigrants in response to the headlines in the newspapers.
The Government is playing a mean spirited type of politics with refugee policy. It could follow an alternative. It could take advantage of the democratic process rather than play to mass audiences through the media and try to take advantage of fear about false refugee claimants and of the frustration felt by immigrants who are trying to reunify their families by bringing relatives to this country legitimately while others are trying to come in through the back-door.
Instead, the Government could implement a generous and genuine policy of family reunification, which it has promised time and time again. There are many immigrant groups in my riding with a genuine need to reunify families in this country. It should do the hard work that is necessary to develop an effective, fair, and generous refugee determination process. No Government can do that by itself. It must conduct public hearings to deal with the current refugee determination process which is clearly ineffective. It takes years to process people through that system. After two years, even if someone were found not to be a legitimate refugee, he has already begun to be integrated into the country and it is difficult to remove him. There are many other reasons the present system does not work. There must be a consultative process to develop a workable and generous refugee determination process.
The Government should produce a paper on its refugee determination policy on which groups concerned about refugee issues can comment. Those groups in our society working with refugee claimants on a daily basis should have input into the policy so that we can develop a process that will work, that will screen out those trying to come in by the back-door and take advantage of the generosity of Canadians, while providing safe haven for legitimate refugees whose lives are in danger for expressing their political views.
A refugee determination process must accomplish two goals. It must separate the wheat from the chaff so that the generosity of Canadians is not taken advantage of, while providing a safe refuge for genuine refugees.
An open door refugee claimant policy would only create a backlash in which Canadians would want to slam the door to prevent abuse of the system. Then we will have hobbled the possibility of establishing a real effective and generous refugee determination system.

June 17, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
The Government should take a democratic approach to the development of a refugee determination policy by allowing public discussion in which the Minister and interested groups can receive attention in the media. That would only be the beginning of the process. Real consultation could take place behind the scenes in which the Minister could have real dialogue with the church groups that work with refugee claimants, with lawyers who work with refugee claimants, with concerned citizens, as well as with members of the Opposition. For instance, the Minister could meet with our critic in order to get the benefit of his consideration in this area and thereby improve the legislation.
The Government has chosen not to do that. Instead, it has taken a much more traditional route of policy development, which is to seize a political opportunity. It has to announce action, strong action which will eradicate this abuse from the system. Therefore the development and the writing of the legislation is conducted behind closed doors. An announcement will come before the legislation is drafted. The call of Parliament will then come before the legislation is even ready. The Government will scramble to put something together. It does not have a real opportunity to meet with people to consider this matter in depth and to obtain some studied comments on the type of policy it is bringing forward.
In choosing to approach the refugee determination question from a political perspective, political in the sense of taking advantage of headlines and trying to get the attention of television cameras, the Government has lost the opportunity to obtain a genuinely democratic policy development process. It has lost the opportunity, thrown it away, to develop a policy in this very difficult area that could actually work, a policy that could combine both compassion and effectiveness.
I know that when the Government made announcements with regard to its legislation it added a footnote with respect to family reunification. It promised a more generous family reunification regime. I assume that it has done this because of what I have heard from people in my riding. I am sure that members of the Government hear the same thing in their ridings. When people from the immigrant communities in my riding go to the Department of Immigration to ask to have a member of their family come to join them, they tell me that it is like banging their head against a brick wall. I am told that the process is very slow and difficult. I know from the case work in my riding that when we seek information from the Department of Immigration to try to assist on some occasions we are successful and we can facilitate the process. However, it is an incredibly slow, cumbersome, and difficult process. There is a need to be more compassionate with regard to those people who are already in this country as immigrants. They are here. They are established. They want to live a decent and humane life. Part of achieving that is by having their whole family here rather than just parts of it.
Rather than the Government stating that it will do something about family reunification as an add-on to an announcement about refugees, it ought to take the whole matter very seriously. It ought to take the opportunity to do something real in the area and to be much more generous in terms of recognizing that families are the backbone of the country. The Government should realize that immigrants have made a great contribution to the country. If we want those immigrants who are here to enjoy the benefits of their own hard work, then we ought to allow them to bring their relatives here.
Rather than seeking to take advantage of headlines and rather than playing to people's fears, the Government ought to be performing some real policy development in the area of family reunification and in the area of developing an effective refugee determination process. In short, it ought to be governing the country. It ought to be developing policies that will work. It ought to be examining the policies that are there, recognizing where the policies do not work, and going through the process of developing a policy that can be effective. That is called governing.
If the present Government were to concern itself more with governing the country than it does with the public opinion polls and the latest headlines, I think it would do better politically. It would do much better in the public opinion polls in the direct result. However, when it seeks, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) appears to be doing most of the time, to play to public opinion and to the headlines as well as to raising of the stature of the Government in the polls, it is seen to be doing just that. The people then simply refuses to give it their confidence. What is needed for the country is a Government that is committed to devising policies that are necessary to meet the problems the country faces.
If the Government were to set its agenda, recognize that we need to have an effective determination policy, and go about developing it, obviously it would receive criticism in the process as well as some publicity. Fundamentally it would build confidence among Canadians in their own capacities, intentions, and values. As an indirect result it would gain in popularity, if we can call it that, and in the polls.
Maybe one of the reasons it is so desperate to use every political opportunity in order to rise in the Gallup poll result is that it was elected on such a wave of public approbation. Members of the Government were so high in the Gallup polls when they were first elected that I am sure it was some sort of a record in polling history. They got so high that when they came crashing down to earth it must have been a pretty hard experience. Thus it desperately sought a quick-fix political answer to its desperate straits in the public opinion polls when what it ought to have been doing was concerning itself with governing the country. Having been elected its job was then to solve the problems that faced Canadians, or at least to face up to them and do the best it could about it.
There is one characteristic about the Government which stands out to a great many Canadians, simply that it does not
June 17, 1988

appear to have a real agenda. It seems to go around like a ping-pong ball. It is battered this way and that. If it could ever establish a real agenda and follow, then people would have confidence in it and it would not have to take political advantage in the area of refugees and immigration.
When the Government was elected it said that it would husband the financial resources of the public. It said that it would be very careful with the way that it would spend money. In the last few days we have seen the Government throwing money around like proverbial drunken sailors. If we could have by-elections in every region of the country, then maybe all Canadians could benefit from this behaviour. What this demonstrates is the fact that the Government has no consistent direction. It just seeks political favour. What we need from the Government is a commitment to govern, to develop the policies that Canadians need and, most particularly, we need a policy with respect to refugee determination.
The hard work that it takes to meet with groups of people and to consult with them in regard to refugee determination legislation and to go through public debate is naturally a part of developing policy in a democratic society. That is what we need from the Government. We need a process that will work, that will be effective and efficient, and that will have compassion.
In light of the fact that so many groups with experience in refugee determination have condemned this legislation, I would ask the Government to withdraw the legislation and start over. It should with a White or Green Paper, throw out some ideas, consult, and start the long, hard work that is necessary to come up with a law that will work.

It is clear that the people who come here as refugees, whether they are from Chile, the Philippines, or another country, are like Canadians. They are good people and like all of us they are unique individuals. Each of us is like a snowflake. We are unique. There are no two people alike. A person's fingerprint is his or her own, no one else's, even though there are now four or five billion people on this planet. Each of the people who come here is unique and has a unique contribution to make to Canada.
These refugees would prefer to stay in their own country and to have made their contribution there, but they did not have that option. Many of the people from Chile live in my riding. Even though they have been here for quite a few years now, they still think of Chile as home. They would like to see democracy return to Chile in order that they could return there.
In the meantime while they are here they are contributing together with other groups to the vitality of our community. We appreciate the uniqueness of each of them and the contribution they make. The fact that each is different and unique provides us with the challenge of understanding. We can appreciate differences in another person, celebrate and enjoy them. At the same time we understand that there is a demand, a requirement that Canadians understand someone who may be different. Of course we are all different and we are all unique.
People from the Philippines have a passionate commitment to democracy. I am sure all Canadians are aware of this fact; they can easily remember the bloodless revolution that took place in the Philippines. The people rose up against a dictatorship and were able to overthrow it and replace it with an electoral democracy. It is incredible witness to the power of the human spirit that, without guns, they were able to overthrow a brutal dictatorship that was abusing their country. Those

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to commence my remarks this afternoon by indicating to the Speaker and to the House that the essence of this Bill is as a result of a problem that commenced one year ago when boat loads of refugees landed on our shores in Atlantic Canada. At that time there was considerable public debate in the nation
with respect to our existing refugee laws. As a result, last summer the Government recalled Parliament to deal with what it termed to be an emergency situation.
What has led us to debate the immigration laws and what has led us to begin the debate today in the final stages of a new refugee law? Perhaps one should go back to our roots as a nation and find ourselves in terms of an historical perspective with respect to the immigration policy Canada has developed since its birth 121 years ago.
I think most Canadians acknowledge that Canada has developed a reputation in the international community as a haven for refugees. Many people have immigrated to this country to build a new life consistent with the values we hold dear to ourselves. From a personal standpoint, I happen to believe that perhaps the reason Canada has such an enviable reputation in the international community is our tolerance for minorities.
I personally believe that our roots in terms of our treatment of minorities go back to the great battle of the Plains of Abraham. For the first time in history, the conqueror allowed the conquered to keep their own language, culture, and system of laws which was quite different from the British system. The French Canadians in Canada at that time accepted the Napoleonic Code of Laws, as they do today.
It was the beginning of Canada as a nation showing much tolerance for minorities. It was the beginning of the development of a reputation that Canada has justly acquired over the years as a country that is very tolerant toward minorities.
If we examine our immigration policy since 1867, we find that there were cycles or waves of immigration beginning in the late 1800s when a number of refugees and immigrants came from the Ukraine. That led to the expansion of Canada, particularly western Canada. In post war years Canada has been very open in terms of its immigration policy to immigrants from Europe and the Third World. I recall the way in which Canadians opened their doors to the people of Hungary during the revolution of 1956 when thousands of Hungarians fled that country because of suppression by a totalitarian regime. They largely fled-and I will elaborate on this with respect to our concerns about this Bill-to a so-called safe country. Most of them fled to Vienna and to Austria, and from Austria they immigrated to other parts of the world. Canada accepted a great many of those Hungarian refugees.
If one looks at the 1960s when we had the Russian invasion of Czechoslovakia, we find that Canada again led the way in the international community by accepting a large number of refugees from Czechoslovakia. One has only to look at the 1970s when we had a similarly grave situation in the Far East. We again opened our hearts and our arms to the boat people.
I think there is a recognition by Canadians that our tolerance toward these refugees has developed our reputation in the international community. The difficulty that has arisen in the last 12 months is that, to some extent, Canadians' faith
June 17, 1988

in the immigration system has been tested. Most Canadians have indicated to Members of Parliament that what they want in terms of a bona fide refugee and immigration law is to ensure that our basic sense of fairness as a nation is being applied and that the integrity of the immigration system is intact. I think that is the prime focus of the review of the existing immigration law. That is the reason we are having this debate in the House of Commons today.
Most Canadians expect their Members of Parliament to ensure when a new immigration law is passed that the sense of integrity of the system and the degree to which Canadians adhere to it, the basic fairness of the Bill, will be addressed by Parliament. This is where the Liberal Party has such difficulties with the legislation presently before the House. We have concerns in three particular areas, namely, the pre-screening section of the Bill, the concept of a safe third country, and the appeal process itself.
It is fundamental that all three political parties acknowledge the need for changes to the existing immigration laws. To some extent, Canadians' faith in the system has been undermined by refugees. I am not talking about bona fide refugees but about refugees with very weak claims who are using the weaknesses in the existing laws to circumvent the system of immigration to this country. Many Canadians feel that, provided genuine refugees are addressed, the rest who are questionable in terms of their bona fide refugee status go through the same process that all other immigrants are expected to follow.
I can go back to the Diefenbaker Government years when the Prime Minister at that time, John Diefenbaker, introduced the Bill of Rights. Subsequently, in the 1981 Constitutional Amendment Prime Minister Trudeau introduced, for the first time in a British parliamentary system, the Charter of Rights. The Charter of Rights, in essence, allows for the supremacy of the individual to take precedence over government. Therefore, it is very important to remember that in the process of passing immigration laws whatever laws we pass ought to be subjected to a test of the principles of the Charter of Rights.
All of us as Members of Parliament should listen to the eminently qualified organizations which have testified not only before the House of Commons committee but before the committee in the other place that dealt in a very compassionate and creative way with the immigration Bill in terms of the amendments it put. To some extent I am very disappointed the Government has chosen to deal with only four of the eighteen amendments recommended by the Senate, but that is the prerogative of the Government.
Surely we must have a great deal of concern when qualified organizations such as the B'nai Brith and the Coalition for a Just Refugee Program indicate to the committees that significant segments of the Bill will contravene the Charter of Rights and Bill of Rights. I believe the test for this Bill should be the application of the Charter of Rights to each and every part of the Bill.
Immigration Act, 1976
Let me now deal with the three major concerns of the Liberal Party with respect to the Bill. I indicated previously that the Senate advocated 18 amendments. Four have been addressed by the Minister and 1 will deal with three of them in my remarks this afternoon.
First, there is a great deal of concern about the prescreening process itself. In terms of the legislation it is a step forward in the creation of a new refugee board that will act at arm's length from the Government to deal with the question of what constitutes a bona fide refugee case and what constitutes a bogus case. However, it seems to me in the process of creating a positive step, namely, the refugee board, we have taken away from the refugee board part of its responsibility by allowing a pre-screening process to take place with an adjudicator and a member of the board. This is ostensibly to cut down on the number of cases that go before the board. That is a major flaw in the Bill. From the standpoint of fairness and equity in the system, it leaves a lot to be desired when at the very beginning of the process two people will be able to determine-and I am sure they will not ask for a long history of the refugee's claim-whether or not a person can then proceed to the refugee board for clarification.
When we talk about a pre-screening process or the application that will come before the refugee board, it is important to realize that in a world in which we have a number of undemocratic regimes large numbers of organizations are seeking autonomy in their own home countries. In effect, we have as we witnessed in the Central American region, death squads of far right and far left ideologies that have terrorized many people and created a large number of people seeking refugee status throughout the world.
Canada has taken a leadership role in immigration, witnessed by the awarding of the Nansen Medal by the United Nations. To some extent this Bill is an abandonment of the principles upon which the Canadian immigration policy and leadership role assumed by Governments, Conservative and Liberal alike over the years, has been founded. By introducing a pre-screening process we have subjected ourselves and are open to the accusation that we say one thing in assuming a leadership role in the international community, but when it comes to this Bill dealing with refugees we are taking away from our advocacy of a just and fair immigration and refugee policy.
With respect to the safe third country concept, the Liberal Party recommended that an arm's length advisory board to Cabinet be established. It would be solely the prerogative and responsibility of the organization at arm's length from the Minister that would be in a position to determine what constitutes a safe third country list. Others have spoken in this House today and previously about the politicization of the process when we allow Cabinet to be the sole arbitrator of what constitutes a safe third country in dealing with a refugee claim.

June 17, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
Let us put this in perspective. People and Members of Parliament have spoken earlier about the United States. All of us assume-and I believe we accept the fact-that the United States will also be a haven for a number of refugee claimants, but even in the United States refugees from El Salvador and from Central America are regularly turned away. Having declared the U.S. to be a safe third country, does it mean that a refugee from El Salvador who claims refugee status in Canada and who commenced his journey to this nation from the U.S. would be deported to El Salvador from the U.S.?
Similarly, in the United Kingdom there has been indiscriminate turning back of Tamil refugees. Would it mean a Tamil who claims refugee status in Canada would be turned back to Britain? Would Britain be considered to be a safe third country?
These questions ought to be clarified before passage of the legislation. The whole concept of a safe third country is an integral part of this legislation. In the international community the concept of a third country list is now accepted. It probably will be the focus of international co-operation in the years to come.
It seems to me that in developing the idea and following through the legislative process it would be much more effective and perceived to be fair and accepted by Canadians, if the decision to determine what constitutes a safe third country were made by a body of experts at arm's length from Cabinet. That is the second point that gives a great deal of concern to us who have been opposed to many parts of the immigration Bill since the Government introduced the draft legislation a year ago.
Much has been made of the fact that in one individual's case the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) intervened and asked that the refugee in question not be granted refugee status. Concern was voiced here in the House of Commons, and it is legitimate. For that very reason the Government ought to accept the amendment to allow the establishment of a body of experts at arm's length from the Government to determine what constitutes a safe third country.
The last area of great concern is the appeal process itself. The appeal process presently in place allows an appeal to take place by a refugee. The appeal goes to the Federal Court of Canada, but the Federal Court can only determine whether the laws of this nation are being applied. The Federal Court is not, in my opinion, the proper place for an appeal process on a refugee claim.
We are not simply talking about questions of law. They are questions of life and death to many refugees. If one looks at history, over the last 10 years those in Iran who practice B'hai have been persecuted. They face death. It is not a question of a point of law. The question is life or death. If a person of the B'hai faith were refused to be considered a bona fide refugee under this legislation, the only point of appeal for that person would be to the Federal Court of Canada, which would only be
able to determine whether or not Canada's laws have been fairly applied. The court would have absolutely nothing to do with the political part of the equation, namely, what constitutes a bona fide refugee claim.
It is important that there be established in the immigration law an appeal process where political points of reference can be applied and tested, and not just simply points of law. Canada has established itself in the international community and has an enviable reputation of being a leader on how to come up with a solution to the refugee problem. This problem gets worse by the day. We have more and more conflicts in various regions of the world that have added to the number of people who will be seeking refugee status. It is important that we have faith in a system that will apply the criteria fairly so that bona fide refugees will be allowed refuge in Canada.
At the same time, at the end of the process of legislative change we also have to ensure that Canadians have faith in the immigration system. I share with all Members of Parliament the concern that to some extent there has been a deterioration in the faith Canadians place in the existing system because people without bona fide refugee status have circumvented the law and have queue jumped. In our haste to solve that problem, we still want to ensure that at the heart of the new law that comes into place, we adhere to the Charter of Rights so that all refugee claimants are dealt with in a fair, just, and compassionate way.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, no one questions the fact that the problem of refugees internationally is a daunting problem demanding an international solution. It is complex. It deals with the lives of thousands, indeed millions of people, who face prosecution, the threat of death, and all manner of dangers and threats to survival.
We also know that Canada has been faced with large numbers of people who have claimed refugee status. There is no doubt that there are those who are not refugees and could lay no credible claim to refugee status who have used our refugee laws to circumvent the immigration process. This is a problem that has been appreciated by all sides. It was a problem that was recognized, for example, by the Employment and Immigration Committee which proposed a new refugee Act that we on this side of the House believe would have addressed the problem adequately and fairly, consistent with international standards and consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Instead of listening to the sound advice submitted by parliamentarians after listening to expert and concerned opinion, the Government introduced Bill C-55 and Bill C-84, Bills which on a number of grounds cause us on this side of the House and many people in Canada a great deal of concern.
June 17, 1988

We heard earlier the exchange that occurred between my colleague, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) and the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) on the issue of racism as it has arisen in this debate. I suppose that if one wanted to encapsulate the kind of exchange that went on, it was that we understand that in this country, racism is not altogether dead. On the other hand, it does not characterize the country as a whole or all of its people. Allegations of racism must be directed with a great deal of care at any portion of the population. At the same time, we must understand that there are a few of us, while not being racist, nevertheless in our efforts to find simple ways of categorizing everyone all too often resort to zenophobic tendencies.
Those of us who are concerned about racism and those of us who have from time to time experienced its ugly effects must conclude that all too often zenophobia, racism, or a kind of vague suspicion that lurks in the hearts of all too many about foreigners, is all too easily exploited for what must be considered crude political purposes.
This concern is only made greater by the fact that we understand that it was not the Portuguese who circumvented the immigration laws and claimed refugee status, nor the Turks who circumvented the immigration laws and claimed refugee status, but the Tamils and Sikhs, sharing only one thing in common apart from the fact that they came by boat, and that is that they are of a different hue, who provoked a strong reaction. There are certainly many of us in Canada who felt that that very strong reaction in those circumstances contained within it far too much zenophobia, perhaps far too much unconscious racism, and certainly a different kind of concern applied to one class of people as compared to another who appeared on our shores.
These kinds of reactions come easily. However, they are reactions that most people, upon a little reflection, hasten to correct. We would hope that a Government would not hasten to exploit such feelings.
There can be no doubt in the minds of those with whom I have talked among the Asian community, the West Indian community, or the African community that these two pieces of legislation would not have appeared under different circumstances. On the other hand, it is a hopeful and encouraging sign that these two pieces of legislation, Bill C-55 and Bill C-84, upon the reflection of the vast majority of Canadians, elicited not support but opposition, opposition to legislation not only because of what provoked it but because of its very character.
I have talked about the opportunism involved in choosing the particular time and circumstances of these two pieces of legislation. One must wonder if there really is a motive that would separate the Government and its legislation on the one hand from those involved in dealing with the refugee problem and the Committee on Employment and Immigration on the other hand.
Immigration Act, 1976
The other day, this debate elicited remarks from the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary, the Hon. Member for Surrey- White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen), who expressed real concern that we might let in too many nihilists, that we might admit too many existentialists, that we may be overburdened by Christian Marxists, that our purity of thought might be affected by dialectical materialists. One wonders if what we are really reflecting in this legislation is some basic attitude toward the kinds of refugees we ought to let in. One wonders whether there is not reflected in those remarks a basic agenda, a kind of selectivity in the minds of those who have brought forth this Bill in terms of who might appropriately be entertained as refugees.
As Hon. Members know, some events have occurred recently that give pause in that they seem to confirm the suspicions elicited by the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary. It has been reported today that one Nota Moises, the information officer of Renamo, is residing in Canada after some rather peculiar concatenation of circumstances that has not favourably affected refugees from Guatemala, El Salvador, and most particularly from India. This is a man who is easily identifiable with the right wing efforts supported by South Africa and the United States in Mozambique which have resulted in the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, with no purpose in mind. As you know, Madam Speaker, the American State Department commissioned a study which ascertained that Renamo had no purpose other than to cause chaos in Mozambique, chaos which had the wide support of right wing factions all over the world. Somehow he found his way into Canada as a refugee, under circumstances which indicate that he circumvented all the rules, and probably, one must suspect, with considerable complicity on both sides of the Atlantic.
On the other hand, let us consider the case of Santokh Singh, an individual whose refugee status was established. He is a legitimate refugee denied admission to this country by virtue of the intervention of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark).
On the one hand we have a legitimate refugee who had his refugee status properly determined having that refugee status determination overruled by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Indeed, there is before us an amendment to this Bill which would make it possible for the action taken by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to be legitimized. This is an unsavoury set of circumstances which we think this legislation will only allow to continue.
We have suspicions with regard to the definition of a safe third country. What is a safe third country? Is it a country which the Secretary of State for External Affairs is concerned will in some way look upon Canada unkindly with respect to our bilateral relationships because we have chosen to act in a legal, humane, and appropriate way in terms of international standards as we did in the case of Santokh Singh? Will our refugee status determination be affected by the peculiar

June 17, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
decisions made by Americans with respect to refugees in the context of their agenda in Central America?
The legislation before us would deprive refugees of a proper determination and a proper basis for an appeal period. In terms of its history and its content, this legislation should be rejected as all too many have suggested it should be. We should, this afternoon, reject this piece of legislation; we should get rid of it.
This piece of legislation, along with another, required us to return here on an emergency basis. It is now a summer later.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry St. Germain (Minister of State (Transport)) moved
speakerposition: Minister of State (Transport)
subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-131, an Act to amend the National Transportation Act, 1987, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport.
He said: Madam Speaker, first I want to thank the opposition for their co-operation in proceeding with this legislation at this time. It is truly a pleasure to rise in the House today and introduce for second reading a Bill which provides the means for ensuring that Canadians with disabilities are provided fair and dignified access to our national transportation system.
Bill C-131, an Act to amend the National Transportation Act, 1987, will give the National Transportation Agency the power to regulate accessibility for disabled persons to all transportation services and facilities under federal jurisdiction.
This will expand on a power that the agency now has to regulate accessibility for the carriage of disabled persons on airlines. The existing power for airlines resulted from an
amendment proposed by the Standing Committee on Transport and concurred with by the former Minister of Transport, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), during hearings held on the Act when it was Bill C-18.
The committee was responding to submissions made to it by representatives of disabled persons, and the Minister of Transport was responding to recommendations from his transportation of disabled persons implementation committee. The Minister's committee included representatives of the industries affected as well as disabled persons.
As a result of the amendments, the agency will be able to prescribe regulations for the purpose of eliminating undue obstacles in transportation to the mobility of disabled persons. By regulation, the agency will be able to establish standards for the design, construction, and modification of means of transportation and related facilities, premises and equipment; respecting the use of signs, for the training of staff; respecting terms and conditions for carrying disabled persons; respecting the communication of information to disabled persons.
The amendments will also provide the enforcement provisions that will enable the agency to make a finding of undue obstacle and order corrective measures and compensation for expenses incurred. They will provide a defence where an applicable regulation has been met or has not been contravened and make the contravention of a regulation an offence which, on summary conviction, will be punishable by up to one year imprisonment and by a fine of up to $5,000 for an individual and by a fine up to $25,000 in the case of a corporation.
I would also point out that the amendments will require the National Transportation Agency and the Canadian Human Rights Commission to co-ordinate their activities in relation to the transportation of disabled persons. Both these agencies, as well as the Office of Privatization and Regulatory Affairs, have been consulted on these amendments.
Accessible transportation is a key to providing persons with disabilities the opportunity for full integration into the mainstream of Canadian life. Accessible transportation provides greater access to housing which, in turn, provides greater opportunities to education. This leads to greater employment opportunities and ultimately to greater selfsufficiency and independence, and the right to lead a full productive life with pride and dignity regardless of one's challenge or age.
The Standing Committee on the Status of Disabled also deserves mention for its tremendous efforts in having the public and private sectors report on activities undertaken to enhance accessibility for disabled persons. In the transportation field, Transport Canada has appeared before the committee and it provides periodic status report on its activities. As well, VIA Rail and Air Canada recently appeared before the committee.
June 17, 1988

The introduction of this Bill today is the culmination of the co-operation of efforts of industry, disabled persons, and government representatives in a true demonstration of how public and private sectors can work together.
The laws of a country are a reflection of the values of its people. I invite Hon. Members today to join with the Government in this co-operative effort so that this legislation can be placed alongside the other laws of Canada that reflect its tradition for protecting human rights and values in Canada.
I have kept my delivery very short so that members of the Opposition can respond. Again, I want to thank opposition Parties for their kind co-operation in dealing with this Bill expeditiously.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the spirit of co-operation, let me indicate to the Minister that the Official Opposition is prepared today to take this Bill to Committee of the Whole and complete third reading stage, if the Government wishes to do so this afternoon.
I want to say a few words about the provisions contained in Bill C-131. They are aimed at improving access for Canada's disabled communities to various passenger transportation services in Canada. As the House is aware, the Liberal Party has consistently supported laws that will improve access to transportation for Canada's handicapped.
In December, 1985, when the Conservative members of the standing committee were waivering to some extent on the principle of improvements for Canada's disabled, the Liberal Party at that time issued a minority report. I want to refer to some passages in the Liberal minority report dated December 18, 1985. We stated that we support all proposed legislation that would increase the accessibility, comfort, safety, and rate structure for the handicapped on all modes of transportation. In particular, we support the prompt implementation of the relevant recommendations of the Equality for All and Obstacles reports.
Our report goes on to say that we want to stress that mandatory minimum safety and access standards for the handicapped be incorporated into the National Transportation Act. The recommendation of the committee only goes as far as saying that the Government states its commitment toward the handicapped. We believe the recommendation should provide that statutory recognition be given to the right of access to transportation modes for the handicapped. Such a statement would legally bind transportation companies to modify their various carriers to ensure accessibility for the handicapped.
National Transportation Act, 1987
I am delighted to say, on behalf of the Official Opposition, that we recognize that Bill C-131 is a step forward for Canada's handicapped. For that reason we would like to have prompt passage of the Bill. I hope that the Minister will take advantage of our good mood this afternoon and proceed to Committee of the Whole and third reading of the Bill.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party and particularly on behalf of the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young) who has been very much involved in all matters relating to disabled people, I would like to say that we, too, wish to see the Bill proceed through all stages this afternoon.
I think that sometimes Canadians who have not had any disability at all fail to realize or have not yet realized that in fact, over three million Canadians are reported to have a disability, according to the Transport Canada study entitled Transportation of Disabled Persons: A Canadian Profile. Almost 70 per cent of all disabilities reported by Canadians 18 years of age and over are related to mobility or agility.
According to another study entitled the Canadian Health and Disability Survey conducted by Statistics Canada, the likelihood of having a disability rises very sharply with age as 38 per cent of Canadians aged 65 and older report a disability. It is therefore very important that we continue to take steps to improve access to those who have a disability. Bill C-131 is an important step in that direction.
